title: Scientists Uncover Massive New Moon Crater, Larger Than Colosseum, From Rare Cosmic Impact
body:
Scientists have identified a previously unknown impact crater on the Moon that dwarfs Earth’s iconic Roman Colosseum, confirming that a “once‑in‑a‑lifetime” collision struck the lunar surface in early 2024. The discovery, made by an international team of planetary geologists using high‑resolution imagery from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and the European Space Agency’s BepiColombo mission, marks the first major crater formation recorded in modern times and offers a rare window into the dynamics of high‑energy impacts on a body without an atmosphere.

The new depression, named “Luna X‑2024” by the research consortium, measures roughly 1.9 kilometres in diameter and plunges about 350 metres deep—dimensions that exceed the 189‑metre span of the Colosseum by a factor of ten. Its sharply defined rim and fresh ejecta blanket indicate an age of less than a year, a conclusion supported by the lack of space‑weathering effects that normally darken lunar features over decades. By analysing the crater’s morphology and the distribution of displaced material, scientists estimate that the impactor was a stony asteroid roughly 30 metres across, striking the Moon at a velocity of 20 kilometres per second.

Such an event is extraordinarily rare. Statistical models of near‑Earth object (NEO) flux suggest that impacts of this magnitude on the Moon occur roughly once every 1–2 million years. The timing, however, coincides with a brief spike in meteoroid activity observed in Earth’s upper atmosphere during March 2024, hinting at a possible fragmenting parent body that sent debris toward both planets. While no corresponding fireball was recorded over Earth’s surface, a faint flash captured by the LRO’s impact monitoring camera aligns precisely with the estimated time of the lunar strike, providing the first direct visual confirmation of a contemporary lunar impact.

Beyond its sheer size, Luna X‑2024 has already begun reshaping scientific understanding of lunar surface processes. The impact generated a localized surge in temperature, temporarily melting regolith and creating a small pool of glassy melt—materials that could be sampled by future robotic missions to study high‑temperature shock metamorphism. Moreover, the ejecta plume altered the albedo of the surrounding terrain, making the area more reflective and potentially affecting the thermal balance of nearby permanently shadowed regions that harbor water ice. Researchers are now modelling how such sudden changes could influence the stability of these ice deposits, a factor of keen interest for upcoming lunar exploration initiatives.

The discovery also underscores the value of continuous lunar surveillance. While Earth’s atmosphere burns up most small meteoroids, the Moon’s barren, airless surface records every collision, acting as a natural laboratory for impact physics. The LRO, which has been orbiting the Moon since 2009, captured the event in a series of rapid‑fire images that were later corroborated by ground‑based telescopes tracking the impact flash. This multi‑instrument approach demonstrates how coordinated observations can detect and characterise impacts that would otherwise go unnoticed, paving the way for a more comprehensive impact catalog in the coming decades.

Looking ahead, Luna X‑2024 is poised to become a focal point for both scientific inquiry and mission planning. NASA’s Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface by the mid‑2020s, could target the crater’s rim for a short‑duration EVA to collect pristine samples of impact melt and ejecta. Such material would provide an unprecedented, “time‑stamp” of a recent high‑energy event, offering insights into crater formation mechanics that have so far been inferred only from ancient, heavily weathered sites. As humanity prepares to establish a sustained presence on the Moon, understanding the frequency and consequences of such impacts will be essential for designing habitats and infrastructure resilient to the occasional, yet potentially disruptive, cosmic collision.
